## Why the Sky Is Blue

Sunlight contains all the colors of the visible spectrum, but when it enters Earth's atmosphere, it collides with gas molecules (primarily nitrogen and oxygen) that are much smaller than the wavelength of light. These tiny particles scatter the incoming light in all directions through a process called **Rayleigh scattering**. Because shorter wavelengths scatter far more strongly than longer ones, the blue and violet ends of the spectrum are redistributed across the sky, so when you look up (away from the Sun directly), you see this scattered light coming from every direction. Interestingly, violet is actually scattered even more than blue, but the sky appears blue rather than violet for two reasons: the Sun emits less violet light to begin with, and our eyes are less sensitive to violet. (This same wavelength dependence explains why sunsets appear red—when sunlight travels through more atmosphere at a low angle, the blue light is scattered away, leaving the longer red wavelengths to reach your eyes.)

## Rayleigh Scattering Wavelength Dependence

The intensity of scattered light is inversely proportional to the **fourth power** of the wavelength:

$$I \propto \frac{1}{\lambda^4}$$

This strong dependence on wavelength is precisely why blue light (shorter λ) scatters much more efficiently than red light (longer λ).
